blocks.html: Introduction

1. Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(\mathfrak{u} = (U_i)_{i \in I}\) a covering of \(X\), which we assume to be either open, or closed and locally finite. If \(\mathfrak{F}\) is an abelian sheaf on \(X\), the Leray spectral sequence: \[ (1.1) \qquad \check{H}^p(\mathfrak{u}, \mathscr{H}^q(\mathfrak{F})) \Longrightarrow H^*(X, \mathfrak{F}) \] defined by \(\mathfrak{u}\) [[5] II (5.2.4) and (5.4.1)] can be described as follows:

The covering \(\mathfrak{u}\) defines a "Čech" resolution \(C^*(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{F})\), functorial in \(\mathfrak{F}\) (ibid. 5.2.1). On the other hand, for every \(\mathfrak{F}\) we have a "canonical flabby" resolution, \(C^*(\mathfrak{F})\), functorial in \(\mathfrak{F}\) (ibid. (4.3)). With these notations, the spectral sequence (1.1) is obtained, in the case where \(\mathfrak{u}\) is open, from the double complex \[ (1.2) \qquad \Gamma(X, C^*(\mathfrak{u}, C^*(\mathfrak{F}))) . \] In the case where \(\mathfrak{u}\) is closed and locally finite, we consider the double complex \[ (1.3) \qquad \Gamma(X, C^*(C^*(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{F}))) . \]

2. Let us seek a unified description of these double complexes. We denote by \(X_o\) the topological space that is the disjoint sum of the \(U_i\), and by \(X_n\) (\(n \geq 0\)) the \((n+1)^{\text{th}}\) iterated fibre product of \(X_o\) with itself over \(X\): \[ (2.1) \qquad X_n = \coprod_{i_0 \dots i_n \in I} U_{i_0} \cap \dots \cap U_{i_n} = \coprod_{\sigma \in \mathrm{Hom}([n], I)} \bigcap_{i=0}^{n} U_{\sigma(i)} . \] The \(X_n\) form a simplicial system of topological spaces, and if \(j_n\) denotes the projection of \(X_n\) onto \(X\), we have \[ (2.2) \qquad C^n(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{F}) = j_{n*}\, j_n^*(\mathfrak{F}) . \] Note that the formation of the canonical flabby resolutions commutes with restriction to an open set and with direct image under a closed immersion. Consequently:

1. a)

    if \(\mathfrak{u}\) is open \[ (2.3) \qquad C^q(\mathfrak{u}, C^p(\mathfrak{F})) = j_{q*}\, j_q^*\, C^p(\mathfrak{F}) = j_{q*}\, C^p(j_q^* \mathfrak{F}) \]

  2. b)

    if \(\mathfrak{u}\) is closed and locally finite \[ (2.4) \qquad C^p(C^q(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{F})) = C^p(j_{q*}\, j_q^* \mathfrak{F}) = j_{q*}\, C^p(j_q^* \mathfrak{F}) . \]

Thus, to obtain a unified description of (1.2) and (1.3), we see that it suffices to take the "canonical flabby" resolution of \(j_q^*(\mathfrak{F})\) on \(X_q\) for every \(q\), and then to apply the functor \(j_{q*}\) to this resolution.

3. The preceding description remains meaningful for any simplicial system of topological spaces over \(X\): \[ (3.1) \qquad \Delta^{o} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Top}/X , \qquad [n] \longmapsto X_n \] not necessarily of the form (2.1). However, the double complex, coaugmented by \(\mathfrak{F}\) \[ (3.2) \qquad \mathfrak{F} \longrightarrow \big(j_{q*}\, C^p(j_q^*(\mathfrak{F}))\big)_{p,q} \] will not in general define a resolution of \(\mathfrak{F}\).

This work is devoted to the search for sufficient conditions for (3.2) to define a resolution of \(\mathfrak{F}\). In this case, the spectral sequence (1.1) generalizes to a spectral sequence \[ (3.3) \qquad \check{H}^p(H^q(X_p, j_p^*(\mathfrak{F}))) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(X, \mathfrak{F}) \] called the "descent spectral sequence".

In the case of "constant coefficients", analogous spectral sequences have been obtained by Segal (cf. [8]), by other methods and for other "cohomology theories", such as K-theory. Segal works in the category of C.W. complexes: he uses a "geometric realization" functor which, to a semi-simplicial complex of topological spaces, associates a new topological space; this new space is to be compared with the topos associated with a simplicial topos [cf. (1.2.12)].

4. In section 5, we illustrate the criteria obtained by constructing, for every analytic space \(X\) over \(\mathbf{C}\), via resolution of singularities, a simplicial system of nonsingular analytic spaces over \(X\), \[ [n] \longmapsto X_n \] such that (3.2) defines a resolution of \(\mathfrak{F}\). If one takes for \(\mathfrak{F}\) the constant sheaf \(\mathbf{C}\), one obtains in particular a spectral sequence \[ (4.1) \qquad H^q(X_p, \mathbf{C}) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(X, \mathbf{C}) \] which expresses the complex cohomology of \(X\) in terms of the complex cohomology of nonsingular analytic spaces. Moreover, if \(X\) is projective, one may assume that all the \(X_p\) are projective: this is the essential ingredient that makes it possible to obtain a kind of "Hodge theory" for \(X\) (cf. [2]).
5. The preceding constructions extend as they stand when one replaces the sheaf \(\mathfrak{F}\) by a bounded-below complex of sheaves. They lead to "localization" techniques in derived categories:

It is known that for \(X_o\) given by (2.1), the map \[ j_o^* : \mathrm{D}^b(X) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}^b(X_o) \] is not faithful in general; we shall show that a datum more precise than that of \(j_o^*(K')\) (for \(K' \in \mathrm{D}^+(X)\)), involving the \(X_n\), sometimes makes it possible to reconstitute the complex \(K'\).

The statements obtained will be used in the appendix of exposé XVII to extend the definition of the functor \(\mathrm{R} f_!\) (\(f\) a separated morphism of finite type between schemes) to the case where \(f\) is not assumed to be compactifiable.

In this application, it is not possible to restrict attention solely to topological spaces, which are here replaced by étale sites of schemes. On the other hand, in order to carry out the proofs, it will be necessary to consider both simplicial systems of spaces and multi-simplicial systems. This explains, justifies, or excuses the degree of hyper-generality from which we shall set out.
1. Preliminaries
1.1 Notations
(1.1.1) In all that follows, \(\mathcal{U}\) is a universe such that \(\mathbf{Z} \in \mathcal{U}\): all the topoi considered will be \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi.

Let \(T\) and \(T'\) be two topoi: a morphism \(\varphi : T \to T'\) consists of the datum of a pair of functors \(\varphi_* : T \to T'\) and \(\varphi^* : T' \to T\), equipped with an adjunction \(\mathrm{Hom}_{T'}(., \varphi_*.) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_T(\varphi^*., .)\), such that \(\varphi^*\) is left exact (i.e. preserves finite projective limits).

Let \((T, \mathcal{O}_T)\) and \((T', \mathcal{O}_{T'})\) be two ringed topoi: a morphism from \((T, \mathcal{O}_T)\) to \((T', \mathcal{O}_{T'})\) is a pair \((\varphi, \theta)\) where \(\varphi : T \to T'\) is a morphism of topoi and \(\theta : \mathcal{O}_{T'} \to \varphi_*(\mathcal{O}_T)\) is a morphism of rings.

(1.1.2) We shall make constant use of the language of fibred categories as it is expounded in [S.G.A. 1 VI]; the reader may also refer to [4]. Let us simply fix some notations: if \(E \to B\) is a fibrant (resp. cofibrant) functor, then for a morphism \(m : i \to j\) in \(B\), we denote by \(m^* : E_j \to E_i\) (resp. \(m_* : E_i \to E_j\)) the associated "inverse image" (resp. "direct image") functor; each of these functors is defined up to a unique functorial isomorphism. If \(\varphi : E \to E'\) is a \(B\)-functor, then for every object \(i\) of \(B\), we denote by \(\varphi_i : E_i \to E'_i\) the functor obtained by restricting \(\varphi\) to \(E_i\).

(1.1.3) Finally, we denote by \(\Delta\) the following category: the objects of \(\Delta\) are the ordered sets \([n] = \{0, 1, \dots, n\}\) and the morphisms of \(\Delta\) are all the increasing maps (in the weak sense). \(\Delta^+\) (resp. \(\Delta^-\)) will denote the category whose objects are those of \(\Delta\) and whose arrows are the monomorphisms (resp. the epimorphisms) of \(\Delta\). We shall freely use, as the need arises, the classical notations introduced in connection with \(\Delta\) [cf. [3] II 2].
1.2 D-topos

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (1.2.1)

Let \(D\) be a category and \(E \to D\) a fibrant and cofibrant functor. We say that \(E\) is bifibred in topoi over \(D\), or that \(E\) is a \(D\)-topos, if the following conditions are satisfied:

  1. (a)

    For every object \(i\) of \(D\), the fibre category \(E_i\) is a topos.

  2. (b)

    For every morphism \(m : i \to j\) in \(D\), there exists a morphism of topoi \(f : E_j \to E_i\) such that \(f_* = m^*\) and \(f^* = m_*\).
Remark. Condition (b) can also be expressed, taking (a) into account, by saying that the functor \(m_*\) is left exact.
When \(D = \Delta\) (resp. \(\Delta \times \Delta\)) we speak of a simplicial (resp. double simplicial) topos to designate a \(\Delta\)-topos (resp. a \(\Delta \times \Delta\)-topos).
In practice, we shall encounter \(D\)-topoi by means of the following considerations:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (1.2.2)

Let \(\mathscr{E}\) be a category fibred and cofibred over \(D\). We say that \(\mathscr{E}\) is bifibred in duals of topoi over \(D\) if \(\mathscr{E}^{o}\) is a \(D^{o}\)-topos.
Explicitly, \(\mathscr{E}\) is bifibred in duals of topoi over \(D\) if and only if the following conditions are satisfied:

1. (a)

    For every object \(i\) of \(D\), the dual category of the fibre category \(\mathscr{E}_i\) is a topos.

  2. (b)

    For every morphism \(m : i \to j\) of \(D\), the functor \(m^*\) is right exact.
(1.2.4) The reader will find in section 4 examples of categories bifibred in duals of topoi.

(1.2.5) Let \(\mathscr{E} \to B\) be a category bifibred in duals of topoi over \(B\) and \(X : D^{o} \to B\) a functor. Then we leave it to the reader to verify that \((D^{o} \times_B \mathscr{E})^{o}\) is a \(D\)-topos, which we shall denote by \(\overline{X}\).

(1.2.6) We shall often say that a functor \(X : D^{o} \to B\) is a \(D\)-object of \(B\) and we denote by \(X_i\) the image under this functor of an object \(i\) of \(D\); the \(D\)-objects of \(B\) form a category denoted \(D^{o}B\). If \(S\) is an object of \(B\), a \(D\)-object of \(B/S\) will be called a \(D\)-object of \(B\) augmented towards \(S\). The datum of a \(D\)-object of \(B\) augmented towards \(S\) is trivially equivalent to the datum of a functorial morphism \(X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) where \(X\) is a \(D\)-object of \(B\) and \(C_S^D\) is the constant \(D\)-object of \(B\) with value \(S\).
When \(D = \Delta\), we speak of a simplicial object (resp. augmented simplicial object).
We shall also use double simplicial objects (by taking \(D = \Delta \times \Delta\)).
(1.2.7) Suppose now that the category \(B\) has finite fibre products.

Let \(f : R \to S\) be an arrow in \(B\): the bifunctor \[ ([n], X) \longmapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ens}}([n], \mathrm{Hom}_S(X, R)) \] from \(\Delta^{o} \times (B/S)^{o}\) to \(\mathrm{Ens}\) defines a functor: \[ [n] \longmapsto X_{[n]} = X_n \] by taking for \(X_n\) a representative of the functor \[ Z \longmapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ens}}([n], \mathrm{Hom}_S(Z, R)) \] \[ \Big(X_n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \overbrace{R \times_S R \times_S \dots \times_S R}^{n+1 \text{ times}}\Big) . \] We denote by \([R\,|_f\,S]\) or \([R\,|\,S]\) the semi-simplicial object augmented towards \(S\) thus constructed.

Finally, let \(X\) and \(X'\) be two semi-simplicial objects of \(B\) (or of \(B/S\)) and \(u : X \to X'\) a functorial morphism. For technical reasons we introduce the object \([X\,|_u\,X']\) computed in the category \(\Delta^{o}B\). The latter is interpreted as a double simplicial object of \(B\), which we then denote by \([[X\,|_u\,X']]\): indeed, we have a canonical isomorphism of categories: \[ \Delta^{o}(\Delta^{o}B) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (\Delta \times \Delta)^{o}B . \] We now return to the general notion of \(D\)-topos.

(1.2.8) Let \(E\) be a \(D\)-topos: we denote by \(\underline{\Gamma}(E)\) the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_D(D, E)\). Let \(f : D' \to D\) be a functor: the category \(D' \times_D E\) is a \(D'\)-topos and, by composition with \(f\), we obtain a functor \[ f^* : \underline{\Gamma}(E) \longrightarrow \underline{\Gamma}(D' \times_D E) . \]

In the case where \(D'\) reduces to a single object \(i\) of \(D\) (with the identity of \(i\) as its only morphism) and \(f\) is the canonical inclusion, denoted \(e_i\), one may take for \(D' \times_D E\) the fibre category \(E_i\), and \(e_i^*\) is then identified with the "evaluation at \(i\)" functor.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (1.2.9)

If \(D'\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category, the functor \(f^*\) has a right adjoint and a left adjoint (denoted respectively \(f_*\) and \(f_!\)).
This follows from a slight generalization of Kan's lemma [III 1.1], of which we shall make constant use.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (1.2.10)

Let \(I\), \(J\) and \(A\) be three categories over a common category \(B\): assume that \(I\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small and that \(A\) is fibred and cofibred over \(B\). We are given a \(B\)-functor \(f : I \to J\), and we denote by \(f^*\) the functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(J, A) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(I, A) \] defined by composition with \(f\). Then, if in each fibre of \(A\) over \(B\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive (resp. projective) limits exist, \(f^*\) has a left adjoint (resp. right adjoint).

Proof. We shall give only the proof of the existence of the left adjoint functor, the resp. part of the lemma following from it by duality. We shall use the following fact, whose verification is left to the reader:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (1.2.10.1)

Let \(A\) be a category bifibred over a category \(B\), \(b\) an object of \(B\) and \((F_\lambda)_{\lambda \in \Lambda}\) a functor from a category \(\Lambda\) to the fibre \(A_b\); then for any \(G\) in \(A_{b'}\) and any \(u : b' \to b\) (resp. \(u : b \to b'\)) in \(B\), we have a bijection: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_u(G, \varprojlim_\lambda F_\lambda) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_\lambda \mathrm{Hom}_u(G, F_\lambda) \] (resp. \(\mathrm{Hom}_u(\varinjlim_\lambda F_\lambda, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_\lambda \mathrm{Hom}_u(F_\lambda, G)\)) whenever the left-hand side is defined.

+ This being so, let \(I \amalg_f J\) be the category over \(B\) defined by: \[ \mathrm{ob}(I \amalg_f J) = \mathrm{ob}(I) \amalg \mathrm{ob}(J) \] \[ \mathrm{Hom}(x,y) = \begin{cases} \mathrm{Hom}_I(x,y) & \text{if } x, y \in \mathrm{ob}(I) \\ \mathrm{Hom}_J(x,y) & \text{if } x, y \in \mathrm{ob}(J) \\ \mathrm{Hom}_J(f(x), y) & \text{if } x \in \mathrm{ob}(I) \text{ and } y \in \mathrm{ob}(J) \\ \varnothing & \text{if } x \in \mathrm{ob}(J) \text{ and } y \in \mathrm{ob}(I) \end{cases} \]

+ The category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(I \amalg_f J, A)\) is equivalent to the category of triples consisting of a \(B\)-functor \(F\) from \(I\) to \(A\), a \(B\)-functor \(G\) from \(J\) to \(A\) and a morphism \(\varphi\) of \(B\)-functors from \(F\) to \(G \circ f\).

+ For every object \(j\) of \(J\), we denote by \(I/j\) the category of objects of \(I\) "placed by \(f\) over \(j\)": the objects of \(I/j\) are the pairs \((i, \alpha)\) where \(i\) is an object of \(I\) and \(\alpha : i \to j\) an arrow of \(I \amalg_f J\), the morphisms of \(I/j\) being those of \(I \amalg_f J/j\). If \(p_I\) and \(p_J\) are the projections of \(I\) and \(J\) onto \(B\), and if \((i, \alpha)\) is an object of \(I/j\), we denote by \(\alpha_* : A_{p_I(i)} \to A_{p_J(j)}\) the functor \(p_J(\alpha)_*\).

+ To give a \(B\)-functor from \(I \amalg_f J\) to \(A\) amounts to giving \(F \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(I, A)\), \(G \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(J, A)\) and a morphism, functorial in \(j\), \[ \psi_j : \varinjlim_{(i,\alpha) \in I/j} \alpha_*(F(i)) \longrightarrow G(j) . \] (The functoriality in \(j\) of the left-hand side follows from (1.2.10.1)). The left adjoint of \(f^*\) is therefore given by the formula: \[ f_!(F)(j) = \varinjlim_{(i,\alpha) \in I/j} \alpha_*(F(i)) \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary (1.2.11)

Let \(E\) be a \(D\)-topos and \(i\) an object of \(D\); the functor \(e_i^*\) admits a left adjoint (resp. a right adjoint), defined by: \[ e_{i!}(a)(j) = \coprod_{\alpha \in \mathrm{Hom}(i,j)} \alpha_*(a) \qquad \Big(\text{resp. } e_{i*}(a)(j) = \prod_{\alpha \in \mathrm{Hom}(j,i)} \alpha^*(a)\Big) \] where \(a\) is an object of \(E\) over \(i\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (1.2.12)

Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category and \(E\) a \(D\)-topos: then the category \(\underline{\Gamma}(E)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos.
+ One verifies "fibre by fibre", using (1.2.10.1), that the category \(\underline{\Gamma}(E)\) has the following properties:

1. a)

    Finite projective limits are representable.

  2. b)

    Direct sums indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) are representable. They are disjoint and universal.

  3. c)

    Equivalence relations are effective and universal.

+ It remains to show that \(\underline{\Gamma}(E)\) has a system of generators indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\): now, if for every object \(i\) of \(D\), \((G_{i\lambda})_{\lambda \in \Lambda_i}\) is a system of generators of \(E_i\) (where \(\Lambda_i\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small set), then the family \((e_{i!}(G_{i\lambda}))_{i,\lambda}\) is a system of generators of \(\underline{\Gamma}(E)\).

(1.2.13) We now introduce the notion of morphism between \(D\)-topoi. Let us first make precise that if \(F\) and \(F'\) are two categories over a common category \(B\) and if \(T : F \to F'\) is a \(B\)-functor, a \(B\)-left adjoint to \(T\) is a functor \(S : F' \to F\), left adjoint to \(T\), such that the canonical morphisms \(1 \to T \circ S\) and \(S \circ T \to 1\) are \(B\)-morphisms of functors. Under these conditions, one trivially verifies that \(T\) is cartesian and that \(S\) is cocartesian.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (1.2.14)

Let \(E\) and \(E'\) be two \(D\)-topoi: a morphism from \(E\) to \(E'\) is a pair of \(D\)-functors \(\Phi_* : E \to E'\) and \(\Phi^* : E' \to E\), equipped with a \(D\)-adjunction \(\mathrm{Hom}(\Phi^*., .) \overset{\xi}{\underset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}} (., \Phi_*.)\), such that for every object \(i\) of \(D\), the pair \((\Phi_{*i}, \Phi_i^*)\), equipped with the adjunction induced by \(\xi\), is a morphism of topoi from \(E_i\) to \(E'_i\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (1.2.15)

Let \(E\) and \(E'\) be two \(D\)-topoi and \((\Phi_*, \Phi^*) : E \to E'\) a morphism. Assume that \(D\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category; then the pair \((\underline{\Gamma}(\Phi_*), \underline{\Gamma}(\Phi^*)) : \underline{\Gamma}(E) \to \underline{\Gamma}(E')\) is a morphism of topoi.
This follows trivially from the preceding definition.
The following lemma, whose proof is left to the reader, makes it possible to construct morphisms of \(D\)-topoi:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (1.2.16)

Let \(E\) and \(E'\) be two categories bifibred over a common category \(D\), and \(\Phi\) a cartesian \(D\)-functor from \(E\) to \(E'\) such that, for every object \(i\) of \(D\), \(\Phi_i : E_i \to E'_i\) has a left adjoint. Then the choice, for every \(i\), of a left adjoint to \(\Phi_i\) canonically determines a \(D\)-functor \(\psi : E' \to E\), a \(D\)-left adjoint to \(\Phi\).

blocks.title: Scholium
blocks.html:
Scholium (1.2.17)

Under the conditions of (1.2.16), suppose that \(E\) and \(E'\) are two \(D\)-topoi and that for every object \(i\) of \(D\), every left adjoint of the functor \(\Phi_i\) is left exact: then, if \(\psi : E' \to E\) is a \(D\)-left adjoint to \(\Phi\), the pair \((\Phi, \psi) : E \to E'\) is a morphism of \(D\)-topoi.

Now let \(\mathscr{E} \to B\) be a category bifibred in duals of topoi over \(B\), \(X\) and \(X'\) two \(D\)-objects of \(B\), and \(\alpha : X \to X'\) a functorial morphism. Then the choice of normalized cleavages for \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(\mathscr{E}^{o}\) determines canonically a morphism \((\alpha_*, \alpha^*) : \overline{X} \to \overline{X}'\) of \(D\)-topoi such that, for every object \(i\) of \(D\), \((\alpha_{*i}, \alpha_i^*) : \overline{X}_i \to \overline{X}'_i\) equals \((\alpha_{i*}, \alpha_i^*)\), where \(\alpha_i : X_i \to X'_i\) is the arrow of \(B\) given by \(\alpha\). For two different choices of cleavages for \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(\mathscr{E}^{o}\), there exists a unique \(D\)-isomorphism between the morphisms thus obtained. (For the verification of these facts, the reader may refer to \([[4] - (1.17)]\)).
1.3 Ringed D-topos

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (1.3.1)

A ringed \(D\)-topos is a pair \((E, A)\) where \(E\) is a \(D\)-topos and \(A\) a ring of \(\underline{\Gamma}(E)\).

One then verifies that for every object \(i\) of \(D\), \(A_i\) is a ring of the topos \(E_i\), and that for every morphism \(m : i \to j\) the canonical arrow \(A_i \to m^*(A_j)\) is a ring homomorphism.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (1.3.2)

Let \((E, A)\) and \((E', A')\) be two ringed \(D\)-topoi: a morphism from \((E, A)\) to \((E', A')\) is a pair \((\Phi, \theta)\) where \(\Phi : E \to E'\) is a morphism of \(D\)-topoi and \(\theta : A' \to \underline{\Gamma}(\Phi_*)(A)\) is a ring homomorphism.

A morphism \(\Phi : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) of ringed \(D\)-topoi induces a morphism \((\underline{\Gamma}(\Phi), \theta) : (\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \to (\underline{\Gamma}(E'), A')\) of ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi when \(D\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category (cf. 1.2.15).

(1.3.4) Let \(\mathscr{E} \to B\) be a category bifibred in duals of topoi over \(B\) and \(\mathfrak{G}\) a ring of \(\underline{\Gamma}(\mathscr{E}^{o}) = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{B^{o}}(B^{o}, \mathscr{E}^{o})\). If \(X : D^{o} \to B\) is a \(D\)-object of \(B\), the \(D\)-topos \(\overline{X}\) (cf. (1.2.5)) is naturally ringed by \((\mathfrak{G} \cdot X)^{o} : D \to \mathscr{E}\), and we denote by \((\overline{X}, \mathfrak{G})\) the ringed \(D\)-topos thus constructed. If \(\alpha : X \to X'\) is a functorial morphism, the morphism \((\alpha_*, \alpha^*) : \overline{X} \to \overline{X}'\) (cf. 1.2.17) induces canonically a morphism \((\overline{X}, \mathfrak{G}) \to (\overline{X}', \mathfrak{G})\) of ringed \(D\)-topoi, again denoted \(\alpha\).

(1.3.5) A ringed \(D\)-topos \((E, A)\) canonically defines a category \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A)\) bifibred in abelian categories over \(D\), whose fibre at an object \(i\) of \(D\) is the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E_i, A_i)\) of modules over the ringed topos \((E_i, A_i)\). With these notations, the category of modules of \(\underline{\Gamma}(E)\) over \(A\), denoted \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\), is identified with the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_D(D, \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A))\).

(1.3.6) Let \(\varphi = (\Phi, \theta) : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) be a morphism of ringed \(D\)-topoi. It defines two functors \(\varphi_* : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A) \to \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E', A')\) and \(\varphi^* : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E', A') \to \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A)\) between the corresponding categories of modules:

- Let \(M\) be an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A)\) over an object \(i\) of \(D\): \(\Phi_*(M)\) is a module over \(\Phi_*(A_i)\) and, by means of the morphism \(\theta_i : A'_i \to \Phi_*(A_i)\), we deduce from it a module over \(A'_i\), denoted \(\varphi_*(M)\). This functor \(\varphi_*\) will be called the direct image functor for the morphism \(\varphi\).

- Let \(M'\) be an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E', A')\) over an object \(i\) of \(D\): \(\Phi^*(M')\) is a module over \(\Phi^*(A'_i)\) and \(\varphi^*(M') = \Phi^*(M') \otimes_{\Phi^*(A'_i)} A_i\) is canonically endowed with a module structure over \(A_i\). By means of (1.2.16), one thus defines a functor \(\varphi^*\), left adjoint to \(\varphi_*\), called the inverse image functor for the morphism \(\varphi\).
(1.3.6.1) We say that \(\varphi\) is flat if the functor \(\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi^*)\) is exact.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (1.3.7)

Let \(f : D' \to D\) be a functor and \((E, A)\) a ringed \(D\)-topos. Then the canonical functor \[ f^* : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E \times_D D'), A \circ f) \] has a right adjoint and a left adjoint if \(D'\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category. In particular, it is exact.

This follows immediately from (1.2.10) and from the identification \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_D(D, \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\).
In accordance with the general notations, we denote by \(f_!\) (resp. \(f_*\)) the left adjoint (resp. right adjoint) of \(f^*\).

(1.3.8) The considerations that follow provide us with a convenient method of computation for the derived functors of the type \(\mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*) : \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \to \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E'), A')\), where \(\varphi : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) is a morphism of ringed \(D\)-topoi (cf. (1.3.6)). [If \((S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) is a ringed topos, we denote by \(\mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) the derived category of the category of \(\mathcal{O}_S\)-modules of \(S\)].
(1.3.9) This formal computation can moreover be applied to other contexts, such as "descent in \(\ell\)-adic cohomology" (cf. S.G.A. 5).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (1.3.10)

Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category. If \((E, A)\) is a ringed \(D\)-topos, we denote by \(I_{(E,A)}\) the set of objects of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\) isomorphic to an object of the form \(\prod_{i \in \mathrm{ob}(D)} e_{i*}(Q_i)\), where, for every object \(i\) of \(D\), \(Q_i\) is totally acyclic (cf. V 4.1)(∗); \(I_{(E,A)}\) satisfies the following properties:

  1. (i)

    For every object \(F\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\) and every object \(i\) of \(D\), \(e_i^*(F)\) is totally acyclic.

  2. (ii)

    Every object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\) injects into an object of \(I_{(E,A)}\).

  3. (iii)

    \(I_{(E,A)}\) is stable under finite direct sums.

  4. (iv)

    For every morphism \(\varphi : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) of ringed \(D\)-topoi, the functor \(\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)\) transforms every acyclic complex of \(C^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\), formed of objects of \(I_{(E,A)}\), into an acyclic complex formed of objects of \(I_{(E',A')}\).
Proof.
(i) Taking into account the explicit expression of \(e_{i*}\) (cf. (1.2.11)), it suffices to prove the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (1.3.10.1)

Let \((S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) be a ringed topos and \((F_t)_{t \in T}\) a family of totally acyclic \(\mathcal{O}_S\)-modules indexed by a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small set \(T\). Then \(\prod_{t \in T} F_t\) is totally acyclic.

Let \(X\) be an object of \(S\): there exists a spectral sequence \[ (1.3.10.2) \qquad H^p\Big(X, \prod_{t \in T}^{(q)} F_t\Big) \Longrightarrow \prod_{t \in T} H^{p+q}(X, F_t) \] where \(\prod_{t \in T}^{(q)}\) denotes the \(q\)-th derived functor of the "product indexed by \(T\)" functor. Since \(\prod_{t \in T}^{(q)} F_t\) is the sheaf associated with the presheaf \(U \longmapsto \prod_{t \in T} H^q(U, F_t)\), (1.3.10.2) degenerates and we obtain isomorphisms \[ (1.3.10.3) \qquad H^n\Big(X, \prod_{t \in T} F_t\Big) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \prod_{t \in T} H^n(X, F_t) \] whence finally \(H^n(X, \prod_{t \in T}) = 0\) for all \(n\).

(ii) Let \(F\) be an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\); for every \(i\) we choose a monomorphism \(F_i \to Q_i\), where \(Q_i\) is totally acyclic in \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E_i, A_i)\): \(e_{i*}(F_i) \to e_{i*}(Q_i)\) is then a monomorphism (since \(e_{i*}\) has a left adjoint), and the canonical arrow: \[ (1.3.10.4) \qquad F \longrightarrow \prod_{i \in \mathrm{ob}(D)} e_{i*}(F_i) \longrightarrow \prod_{i \in \mathrm{ob}(D)} e_{i*}(Q_i) \] is again a monomorphism, as one trivially verifies.
(iii) Proof left to the reader.

(iv) We also leave it to the reader to verify that \(\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)\) transforms an object of \(I_{(E,A)}\) into an object of \(I_{(E',A')}\). Once this point is established, it suffices, taking (i) into account, to verify the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (1.3.10.5)

If \(0 \to F \to G \to H \to 0\) is a short exact sequence in \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\), with \(F \in I_{(E,A)}\) and \(G \in I_{(E,A)}\), then the sequence \(0 \to \underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)(F) \to \underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)(G) \to \underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)(H) \to 0\) is exact in \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E'), A')\).

It suffices to note that \(e_i^*(H)\) is acyclic for every object \(i\) of \(D\) and that the computation of \(\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)\) is carried out fibre by fibre, which completes the proof of (1.3.10).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary (1.3.11)

Let \(\varphi : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) be a morphism of ringed \(D\)-topoi. One can compute the functor \(\mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)\) by means of resolutions formed of objects of \(I_{(E,A)}\).

Let \(L \subset K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\) be the full subcategory of complexes formed of objects of \(I_{(E,A)}\): \(L\) is a triangulated subcategory by virtue of ((1.3.10), (ii)), and we can apply to it theorem (5.1) of \([[7] - \text{Chap.1}]\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary (1.3.12)

Let \(\varphi : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) be a morphism of ringed \(D\)-topoi; for every object \(i\) of \(D\) we denote by \(\varphi_i : (E_i, A_i) \to (E'_i, A'_i)\) the morphism of ringed \(D\)-topoi induced by \(\varphi\) over \(i\). Then the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{R}^+(e_i^*)} \ar[d]_{\mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)} & & \mathrm{D}^+(E_i, A_i) \ar[d]^{\mathrm{R}^+\varphi_{i*}} \\ \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E'), A') \ar[rr]_-{\mathrm{R}^+(e_i^*)} & & \mathrm{D}^+(E'_i, A'_i) } \] is essentially commutative.

We have a morphism \[ \mathrm{R}^+(e_i^*) \circ \mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*) \longrightarrow \mathrm{R}^+\varphi_{i*} \circ \mathrm{R}^+(e_i^*) \] which one verifies to be an isomorphism, by virtue of (1.3.10).

We denote by \(G_{(E,A)}\) the set of objects \(F\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\) such that \(e_i^*(F)\) is totally acyclic for every object \(i\) of \(D\). It follows from the proof of (1.3.10) that one can compute \(\mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\varphi_*)\) by means of resolutions formed of objects of \(G_{(E,A)}\); this is what one does in particular in the introduction, using the "canonical flabby resolution"(∗). According to \([(1.3.10)(i)]\), we have \(I_{(E,A)} \subset G_{(E,A)}\), but we shall explicitly use \(I_{(E,A)}\) in section 2.

footnotes.html: (∗) cf. exposé XVII for the generalization of this notion.

blocks.html: 2. The method of cohomological descent
In this section, \(D\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category.
2.1 Generalities. Notations

(2.1.1) Let \((S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) be a ringed topos. The category \(S \times D\), equipped with the canonical projection \(S \times D \to D\), is a \(D\)-topos; moreover, the section with constant value \(\mathcal{O}_S\) defines a ringed \(D\)-topos \((S \times D, \mathcal{O}_S)\), called the \(D\)-topos ringed and constant with value \((S, \mathcal{O}_S)\). With these notations, the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S)\) is identified with the category of covariant functors from \(D\) to \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\).

We define an exact functor: \[ \varepsilon^* : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S) \] by associating with each module \(F\) over \(S\) the constant functor with value \(F\). The functor \(\varepsilon^*\) has a right adjoint \(\varepsilon_*\) which associates with each functor \(H : D \to \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathcal{O}_S)\) its projective limit, the adjunction morphism \(F \to \varepsilon_* \varepsilon^*(F)\) being the one that sends \(F\) to the projective limit of the constant functor with value \(F\); thus \(\varepsilon^*\) is fully faithful if and only if \(D\) is connected.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.1.2)

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed \(D\)-topos; an augmentation of \((E, A)\) is a morphism (of ringed \(D\)-topoi) from \((E, A)\) to a constant ringed \(D\)-topos. A ringed \(D\)-topos equipped with an augmentation will be called an augmented ringed \(D\)-topos.

(2.1.3) Let \(\mathscr{E} \to B\) be a category bifibred in duals of topoi, and \(\mathfrak{G}\) a ring of \(\underline{\Gamma}(\mathscr{E}^{o}) = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{B^{o}}(B^{o}, \mathscr{E}^{o})\). Let \(S\) be an object of \(B\): a functor \(D^{o} \to B/S\), that is, a functorial morphism \(X \xrightarrow{\ \theta\ } C_S^D\), where \(X\) is a functor \(D^{o} \to B\) (cf. (1.2.6)), induces an augmentation: \[ \theta : (\overline{X}, \mathfrak{G}) \longrightarrow (\mathscr{E}_S^{o} \times D, \mathfrak{G}_S) \qquad \text{(cf. (1.3.4))}, \] which we shall denote by the same letter as the functorial morphism that gives rise to it.
2.2 Cohomological descent

(2.2.1) Let \(\theta : (E, A) \longrightarrow (S \times D, \mathcal{O}_S)\) be an augmented ringed \(D\)-topos; we set, with the notations of (1.3.6) and (2.1.1), \[ \overline{\theta}^* = \underline{\Gamma}(\theta^*) \circ \varepsilon^* : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \] and \[ \overline{\theta}_* = \varepsilon_* \circ \underline{\Gamma}(\theta_*) : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(S, \mathcal{O}_S) . \] The image of \(\overline{\theta}^*\) lies in the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\) formed by the cocartesian sections of \(\underline{\Gamma}(D, \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A))\): we shall denote this last category by \(\underline{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{cocart}}(D, \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A))\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.2.2)

We say that \(\theta\) is an augmentation of effective descent if \(\underline{\Gamma}(\theta^*) \circ \varepsilon^* : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow \underline{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{cocart}}(D, \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A))\) is an equivalence of categories.

(2.2.3) With the notations of (2.2.1), suppose that \(\theta\) is flat, so that \(\overline{\theta}^*\) is exact and passes trivially to the derived categories: let \(\mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*)\) be the functor thus obtained. With these notations:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (2.2.3.1)

There exist two functorial morphisms \[ \alpha : \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*) \circ \mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*) \quad \text{and} \quad \beta : \mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*) \circ \mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*) \longrightarrow \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)} \] putting these two functors in adjunction.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.2.4)

We say that \(\theta\) is an augmentation of cohomological 1-descent if

  1. 1°)

    \(\theta\) is flat

  2. 2°)

    The functor \(\mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*)\) is fully faithful.
Condition 2°) of the preceding definition can also be expressed by saying that the morphism \(\alpha\) in (2.2.3.1) is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.2.6)

We say that \(\theta\) is an augmentation of cohomological 2-descent (or of effective cohomological descent) if \(\theta\) is at once an augmentation of effective descent and an augmentation of cohomological 1-descent.
The preceding terminology is justified by the following result:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.2.7)

Let \(\theta\) be an augmentation of effective cohomological descent. Then the essential image of \(\mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*)\) is the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\) formed by the complexes \(F'\) such that for every \(i\), \(H^i(F')\) is a cocartesian section of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(E, A)\).

We shall say, for brevity, that a complex \(F'\) satisfying the preceding conditions is a cohomological descent datum. It is clear that if \(K' \in \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\), then \(\mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*)(K')\) is a cohomological descent datum: it therefore suffices to show that for every cohomological descent datum \(F'\), the canonical morphism \[ \beta(F') : \mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*) \circ \mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(F') \longrightarrow F' \] is an isomorphism in \(\mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A)\).
a) Case where \(F'\) is bounded: we argue by induction on the length \(\ell\) of the interval of integers \(i\) where \(H^i(F') \neq 0\):
- for \(\ell \leq 1\) the assertion is true because \(\theta\) is of effective descent.

- suppose \(\ell > 1\) and let \(n\) be the largest integer such that \(H^n(F') \neq 0\): we have a distinguished triangle(∗) \[ \xymatrix@C=1em@R=2.5em{ & H^n(F')[-n] \ar[dl] & \\ F'' \ar[rr] & & F' \ar[ul] } \] such that the induction hypothesis applies to \(F''\); since \(\beta(H^n(F')[-n])\) and \(\beta(F'')\) are isomorphisms, the same holds for \(\beta(F')\).

b) General case: we denote by \(\sigma_{\leq n}(F')\) the complex \[ \cdots \longrightarrow F^{n-2} \longrightarrow F^{n-1} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ker} d^n \longrightarrow 0 \longrightarrow 0 \longrightarrow \cdots , \] (cf. [7] (7.1)), so that for every \(n\) we have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*) \circ \mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(\sigma_{\leq n}(F')) \ar[rr]^-{\sim} \ar[d] & & \sigma_{\leq n}(F') \ar[d] \\ \mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*) \circ \mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(F') \ar[rr] & & F' } \] and it suffices to check that the morphism \[ \mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(\sigma_{\leq n}(F')) \longrightarrow \mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(F') \] induces an isomorphism on the \(H^i\) for \(i \leq n\). Now, we have a triangle: \[ \xymatrix@C=1em@R=2.5em{ & F''' \ar[dl] & \\ \sigma_{\leq n}(F') \ar[rr] & & F' \ar[ul] } \] with \(H^i(F''') = 0\) for \(i \leq n\). We then deduce that \(H^i(\mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(F''')) = 0\) for \(i \leq n\), and then that \(H^i(\mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(\sigma_{\leq n}(F'))) \longrightarrow H^i(\mathrm{R}^+(\overline{\theta}_*)(F'))\) is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n\), which completes the proof.

We shall now present a method for the explicit computation of \(\mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_*\) that is very useful in the proof of certain criteria for cohomological descent, as well as in the exploitation of this notion.
2.3 A computational procedure for \(\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_*\)
We shall begin with two sorites.

(2.3.1) Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category and \(\mathrm{Ab}\) the category of abelian groups belonging to \(\mathcal{U}\). We denote by \(r_D\) the functor \(D \to (\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab}))^{o}\) defined by the relation \[ r_D(i)(j) = \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{Hom}(i,j)} \] for every pair \((i, j)\) of objects of \(D\). We then construct, for every pair \((i, X)\) consisting of an object of \(D\) and an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab})\), a canonical and functorial isomorphism: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(r_D(i), X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X(i) \]

(2.3.1.1) Let \(A\) be an additive category (cf. Tohoku) and \(F\) a functor \(D \to A\): we define a functor \(\overline{F} : (\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab}))^{o} \longrightarrow A^{o}\mathrm{Ens}\) by the relation \[ \overline{F}(X)(a) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab})}(X, \mathrm{Hom}_A(a, F(.))) \] so that the following diagram, in which \(h_A\) denotes the canonical functor: \[ \xymatrix{ D \ar[rr]^-{r_D} \ar[d]_{F} & & (\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab}))^{o} \ar[d]^{\overline{F}} \\ A \ar[rr]_-{h_A} & & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(A^{o}, \mathrm{Ens}) } \] is essentially commutative.

We leave it to the reader to verify that \(\overline{F}\) transforms the finite direct sums of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab})\) into products and that, if we denote by \(\mathbf{Z}\) the constant functor \(D \to \mathrm{Ab}\) with value \(\mathbf{Z}\), we have \(\overline{F}(\mathbf{Z}) = \varprojlim F\).

Finally, the correspondence \(F \rightsquigarrow \overline{F}\) defines a covariant functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, A) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}((\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab}))^{o}, \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(A^{o}, \mathrm{Ens})) . \]

(2.3.1.2) We denote by \(\mathrm{Add}(D)\) the full subcategory of \((\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab}))^{o}\) defined by the objects of the form \(r_D(i)\), where \(i\) is an object of \(D\), and their finite direct sums. The category \(\mathrm{Add}(D)\) is additive and the functor \(r_D : D \to \mathrm{Add}(D)\) satisfies the following universal property:

(2.3.1.3) For every additive category \(A\), the functor \(G \longmapsto G \circ r_D\) induces an equivalence from the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathrm{Add}(D), A)\) formed by the additive functors onto the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, A)\).
The category \(\mathrm{Add}(D)\), defined up to equivalence by (2.3.1.3), will be called the additive category generated by \(D\).

(2.3.2) Let \(A\) be an abelian category and \(K''\) a double complex which we regard as an object of \(C^+(C^+(A))\), the first index corresponding to the first symbol \(C^+\): we denote by \((K'')_s\) the associated simple complex (cf. Tohoku (2.4), whose notation we shall retain). We thus define a functor \[ (2.3.2.1) \qquad (\ )_s : C^+(C^+(A)) \longrightarrow C^+(A) \] and we leave it to the reader to verify the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (2.3.2.2)

The functor \((\ )_s\) defines a triangulated functor: \[ K^+(C^+(A)) \longrightarrow K^+(A) \] which preserves quasi-isomorphisms; it therefore defines a triangulated functor: \[ \mathrm{D}^+(C^+(A)) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}^+(A) , \] again denoted \((\ )_s\).
Remark. We have the same result for the functor \((\ )_s : C(C^b(A)) \to C(A)\) because the spectral sequence under consideration is biregular by (E.G.A. III (11.3.3)).

(2.3.3) This being so, let \((S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) be a ringed topos and \(D\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category. Let \(Z' \in C^+(\mathrm{Add}(D))\) be a cochain complex such that \(Z^n = 0\) for \(n < 0\).

Every object \(F\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D, \mathcal{O}_S), \mathcal{O}_S)\) (which is identified with a functor \(D \to \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) by (2.1.1)) defines, via the universal property of \(\mathrm{Add}(D)\), an object \(\varepsilon_{Z'*}(F)\) of \(C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) which varies functorially with \(F\) by (2.3.1.3).

We thus define a triangulated functor: \[ (2.3.3.1) \qquad K^+(\varepsilon_{Z'*}) : K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow K^+(C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)) . \] Moreover, it follows from (2.3.2.2) that the composite functor: \[ (\ )_s \circ K^+(\varepsilon_{Z'*}) : K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow K^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \] transforms acyclic objects into acyclic objects. It therefore defines a triangulated functor: \[ (2.3.3.2) \qquad \mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} : \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \] satisfying the relation \(Q \circ (\ )_s \circ K^+(\varepsilon_{Z'*}) = \mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} \circ Q\)(∗).

(2.3.4) The preceding data are retained. We regard \(Z'\) as a chain complex in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D, \mathrm{Ab})\). Let \(t : Z^{0} \to \mathbf{Z}\) be a morphism from \(Z^{0}\) to the constant functor with value \(\mathbf{Z}\) such that the composite morphism \[ (2.3.4.1) \qquad Z^1 \longrightarrow Z^{0} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } \mathbf{Z} \] is zero.

By functoriality (cf. (2.3.1.1)), we deduce from this a morphism \(\varepsilon_*(F) \to \varepsilon_{Z'*}(F)^{0}\) such that the composite morphism \[ (2.3.4.2) \qquad \varepsilon_*(F) \longrightarrow \varepsilon_{Z'*}(F)^{0} \longrightarrow \varepsilon_{Z'*}(F)^{1} \] is zero.

There then exists a canonical morphism of triangulated functors: \[ (2.3.4.3) \qquad Q \circ K^+(\varepsilon_*) \xrightarrow{\ j\ } Q \circ (\ )_s \circ K^+(\varepsilon_{Z'*}) = \mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} \circ Q \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.3.5)

The conditions and notation of (2.3.3) and (2.3.4) are retained; we assume moreover that the augmented complex \[ Z^n \longrightarrow Z^{n-1} \longrightarrow \cdots \longrightarrow Z^1 \longrightarrow Z^{0} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } \mathbf{Z} \] defines a resolution of \(\mathbf{Z}\).

Then, for every complex \(F'\) formed of objects of \(I_{(S \times D, \mathcal{O}_S)}\) (cf. 1.3.10), \[ j(F') : Q \circ K^+(\varepsilon_*)(F') \longrightarrow (\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} \circ Q)(F') \] is an isomorphism.

+ Let \(i\) be an object of \(D\) and \(Q_i\) a module over \((S, \mathcal{O}_S)\): let us show that \(j(e_{i*}(Q_i))\) is an isomorphism. We must check that the sequence: \[ (2.3.5.1) \qquad 0 \longrightarrow Q_i \longrightarrow \varepsilon_{Z'*}(e_{i*}(Q_i))^{0} \longrightarrow \varepsilon_{Z'*}(e_{i*}(Q_i))^{1} \longrightarrow \cdots \] is exact.

For this it suffices to show that, for every object \(X\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\), the sequence: \[ (2.3.5.2) \quad 0 \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, Q_i) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, \varepsilon_{Z'*}(e_{i*}(Q_i))^{0}) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, \varepsilon_{Z'*}(e_{i*}(Q_i))^{1}) \to \cdots \] is exact. Now an immediate computation shows that (2.3.5.2) reduces to: \[ (2.3.5.3) \quad 0 \to \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{Z}, \mathrm{Hom}(X, Q_i)) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Add}(D)}(Z^{0}, i), \mathrm{Hom}(X, Q_i)) \to \] \[ \to \mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Add}(D)}(Z^{1}, i), \mathrm{Hom}(X, Q_i)) \to \cdots . \]

+ If, for every object \(i\) of \(D\), \(Q_i\) is a totally acyclic module, then we see, by applying the functor \(\prod_{i \in \mathrm{ob}(D)}\) to the complexes (2.3.5.1), that we again obtain an acyclic complex by (1.3.10.1). Thus \(j(\prod_{i \in \mathrm{ob}(D)} e_{i*}(Q_i))\) is an isomorphism.
+ We leave it to the reader to deduce from this that \(j(F')\) is an isomorphism when \(F^n \in I_{(S \times D, \mathcal{O}_S)}\) for all \(n\) (by spectral sequences, for example).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary (2.3.6)

Under the conditions of (2.3.5), the morphism \(j\) defines \(\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*}\) as the derived functor of \(\varepsilon_*\).

The subcategory of \(K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S)\) defined by the complexes formed of objects of \(I_{(S \times D, \mathcal{O}_S)}\) satisfies the conditions of theorem (5.1) of \([[7], I]\), for the functor \(K^+(\varepsilon_*)\), by virtue of (1.3.10) and (2.3.5): the corollary follows immediately from this remark.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary (2.3.7)

Under the conditions of (2.3.5), let \((E, A)\) be a ringed \(D\)-topos and \(\theta : (E, A) \to (S \times D, \mathcal{O}_S)\) an augmentation; there exists a canonical isomorphism \[ \mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\theta_*) \circ \mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} . \]
This follows from \([[7] - I - 5.4]\).

We knew a priori that \(\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_*\) exists and that we have an isomorphism \(\mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\theta_*) \circ \mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_*\), since \(\underline{\Gamma}(\theta_*)\) and \(\varepsilon_*\) are induced by morphisms of ringed topoi (cf. (1.3.6) and (2.1.1)). Nevertheless the preceding computation will prove very useful and applicable to other contexts, for, in practice, the conditions of (2.3.5) will always be satisfied.
We shall now give the fundamental examples in which (2.3.5) can be applied.

(2.3.9) In \(\mathrm{Add}(\Delta)\), we set \(Z^n = [n]\) and we define \(d^n : Z^n \to Z^{n+1}\) by the formula \[ (2.3.9.1) \qquad d^n = \sum_{i=0}^{n+1} (-1)^i \partial^i \] where \(\partial^i : [n] \to [n+1]\) is the \(i\)-th face [cf. [3] II 2]. For \(t : Z^{0} \to \mathbf{Z}\) we take the obvious natural augmentation.
The condition of (2.3.4) is trivially satisfied. The condition of (2.3.5) follows from ([5] I (3.7.4)).

(2.3.10) In \(\mathrm{Add}(\Delta \times \Delta)\), we consider the simple complex associated with the double complex: \[ (2.3.10.1) \qquad \xymatrix{ ([n], [m+1]) \ar[rr]^-{s_1^{n,m+1}} & & ([n+1], [m+1]) \\ ([n], [m]) \ar[rr]_-{s_1^{n,m}} \ar[u]^{s_2^{n,m}} & & ([n+1], [m]) \ar[u]_{s_2^{n+1,m}} } \] with \[ (2.3.10.2) \qquad \begin{cases} s_1^{n,m} = \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n+1} (-1)^i (\partial^i, \mathrm{id}_{[m]}) \\[1.5ex] s_2^{n,m} = \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m+1} (-1)^j (\mathrm{id}_{[n]}, \partial^j) . \end{cases} \] We leave it to the reader to verify (using (2.3.9)) that the complex thus defined, equipped with the obvious natural augmentation, satisfies the conditions of (2.3.5).
(2.3.11) The multi-simplicial case is treated analogously (with \(\underbrace{\Delta \times \Delta \times \dots \times \Delta}_{p\text{-times}}\)).
2.4 Relative cohomological descent
(2.4.0) Let \(\mathscr{E} \to B\) be a category bifibred in duals of topoi and \(\mathfrak{G}\) a ring of \(\underline{\Gamma}(\mathscr{E}^{o})\).

These data canonically define a category fibred and cofibred in abelian categories, denoted \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}^{o}, \mathfrak{G})\), over \(B^{o}\) (cf. (1.3.3) and (1.3.4)): in all that follows, the "direct image" and "inverse image" functors will always be taken with respect to the fibring and cofibring functor: \[ \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}^{o}, \mathfrak{G}) \longrightarrow B^{o} . \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.4.0.1)

We shall say that a morphism \(f : T \to S\) in \(B\) is flat (relatively to \((\mathscr{E}, \mathfrak{G})\)) if \(f_* : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}_S^{o}, \mathfrak{G}_S) \to \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}_T^{o}, \mathfrak{G}_T)\) is an exact functor.

(2.4.1) Let \(G\) be a subcategory fibred and cofibred of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}^{o}, \mathfrak{G})\) such that, for every object \(S\) of \(B\), \(G_S\) is a thick subcategory (cf. Tohoku (1.11)) of \((\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}^{o}, \mathfrak{G}))_S\) — The reader will find in section 4 examples of such situations.

If \(S\) is an object of \(B\), we shall denote by \(\mathrm{D}^+(S)\) the derived category of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}_S^{o}, \mathfrak{G}_S)\): following \([[7]\ (I\ \S\ 4)]\), we introduce the category \(\mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)\), which is identified with the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{D}^+(S)\) formed by the objects \(X'\) such that \(H^n(X') \in G_S\) for all \(n\).
We shall assume that the following condition is always satisfied.

(2.4.1.1) For every morphism \(h : T \to S\) in \(B\), the functor \(\mathrm{R}^+(h^*) : \mathrm{D}^+(T) \to \mathrm{D}^+(S)\) is such that \(\mathrm{R}^+(h^*)(F) \in \mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)\) if \(F \in G_T\).
By \([[7]\ (I.\ (7.3).(ii))]\), this condition implies that \(\mathrm{R}^+(h^*)(\mathrm{D}_{G_T}^+(T)) \subset \mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)\).

(2.4.2) Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category: we shall assume in all that follows that we are given a complex \(Z'\) of \(\mathrm{Add}(D)\) satisfying the conditions of (2.3.5) (in the applications, we shall in fact have \(D = \Delta\) or \(D = \Delta \times \Delta\)).

If \(X : D^{o} \to B\) is a \(D\)-object of \(B\), we denote by \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}_G(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) formed by the objects \(F\) such that \(e_i^*(F) \in G_i\ (= G_{X_i})\) for every object \(i\) of \(D\): \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}_G(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) is a thick subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\). We shall denote by \(K_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) (resp. \(\mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\)) the full subcategory of \(K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) (resp. \(\mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\)) formed of the objects \(X'\) such that \(H^n(X') \in \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}_G(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) for all \(n\).

(2.4.3) Let \(X\) and \(X'\) be two \(D\)-objects of \(B\) and \(\alpha : X \longrightarrow X'\) a functorial morphism. Recall (cf. (1.3.4)) that we again denote by \(\alpha : (\overline{X}, \mathfrak{G}) \longrightarrow (\overline{X}', \mathfrak{G})\) the corresponding morphism of ringed \(D\)-topoi.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.4.3.1)

We shall say that \(\alpha : X \to X'\) is flat if the corresponding morphism of \(D\)-ringed topoi is flat in the sense of (1.3.6.1).
We then have the obvious lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (2.4.3.2)

For \(\alpha : X \to X'\) to be flat, it is necessary and sufficient that, for every object \(i\) of \(D\), \(\alpha_i : X_i \to X'_i\) be a flat morphism (cf. (2.4.0.1)).

(2.4.4) Let \(\alpha : X \to X'\) be a morphism; it defines a functor \[ (2.4.4.1) \qquad K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\alpha_*)) : K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G}) \longrightarrow K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}'), \mathfrak{G}) . \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (2.4.4.2)

The functor \[ K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\alpha_*)) \big|\, K_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G}) : K_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G}) \longrightarrow K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}'), \mathfrak{G}) \] possesses a right derived functor, denoted \(\mathrm{R}_G^+\underline{\Gamma}(\alpha_*)\), and the canonical morphism \[ \mathrm{R}_G^+\underline{\Gamma}(\alpha_*) \longrightarrow \mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\alpha_*) \big|\, \mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G}) \] is a morphism.

Moreover \(\mathrm{R}_G^+(\mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})) \subset \mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}'), \mathfrak{G})\).

The first part follows from (1.3.10) and from \([[7] - (I.(5.2))]\). To verify the last assertion, it suffices to show, by virtue of \([[7] - (I.7.3).(ii)]\), that \(\mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\alpha_*)(F) \in \mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}'), \mathfrak{G})\) when \(F \in \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}_G(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\), which follows from the explicit computation of \(\mathrm{R}^+\underline{\Gamma}(\alpha_*)\) given by (1.3.11) and from hypothesis (2.4.1.1).

(2.4.5) Let \(S\) be an object of \(B\): the ringed \(D\)-topos \((\overline{C_S^D}, \mathfrak{G})\) (cf. (1.2.6)) is identified with the constant ringed \(D\)-topos \((\mathscr{E}_S^{o} \times D, \mathfrak{G}_S)\) and we have the following lemma which follows from \([[7](I.7.3).(ii))]\):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (2.4.5.1)

The functor \(\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} \big|\, \mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{C_S^D}), \mathfrak{G})\), denoted \(\mathrm{R}_G^+\varepsilon_{Z'*}\), takes its values in \(\mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)\) and is identified with a right derived functor of the functor \[ K^+(\varepsilon_*) \big|\, K_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{C_S^D}), \mathfrak{G}) : K_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{C_S^D}), \mathfrak{G}) \longrightarrow K^+(S) . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.4.6)

Let \(\theta : X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) be an augmented \(D\)-object of \(B\): the functor \(K^+(\overline{\theta}_*) \big|\, K_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) possesses a right derived functor, denoted \(\mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{\theta}_*\), which takes its values in \(\mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)\). Moreover, there exists a canonical isomorphism \[ \mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{\theta}_* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{R}_G^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} \circ \mathrm{R}_G^+\underline{\Gamma}(\theta_*) . \]
Proof left to the reader on the basis of what precedes.
We are now in a position to give the definitions relating to cohomological descent.

(2.4.7) Let \(\theta : X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) be an augmented \(D\)-object of \(B\). Suppose that \(\theta\) is flat, so that the restriction to \(\mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)\) of the functor \(\mathrm{L}^+\overline{\theta}^*\) takes its values in \(\mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\): we shall denote by \(\mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{\theta}^*\) this restriction. With this notation:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (2.4.7.1)

There exist two functorial morphisms \(\alpha : \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)} \to \mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{\theta}_* \circ \mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{\theta}^*\) and \(\beta : \mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{\theta}^* \circ \mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{\theta}_* \longrightarrow \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})}\) placing these two functors in adjunction.
This follows immediately from (2.2.3.1) and (2.4.6).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.4.8)

We say that \(\theta\) is an augmentation of cohomological 1-descent relatively to \(G\) if

  1. 1°)

    \(\theta\) is flat.

  2. 2°)

    The functor \(\mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{\theta}^*\) is fully faithful.
Condition 2°) of the preceding definition can also be expressed by saying that the morphism \(\alpha\) in (2.4.7.1) is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.4.10)

Let \(\theta : X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) be an augmented \(D\)-object of \(B\). We say that \(\theta\) is an augmentation of effective descent relatively to \(G\) if the functor \[ \underline{\Gamma}(\theta^*) \circ \varepsilon^* : G_S \longrightarrow \underline{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{Cocart}}(D, G) \] is an equivalence of categories.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.4.11)

We say that \(\theta\) is an augmentation of cohomological 2-descent (or of effective cohomological descent) relatively to \(G\) if \(\theta\) is at the same time an augmentation of cohomological 1-descent and of effective descent relatively to \(G\).
From the proof of (2.2.7) we then deduce the following result:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem (2.4.12)

Let \(\theta : X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) be an augmentation of cohomological 2-descent relatively to \(G\). Then the essential image of \(\mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{\theta}^*\) is the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{D}_G^+(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{X}), \mathfrak{G})\) formed of the complexes \(F'\) such that for every \(n\), \(H^n(F')\) is a cocartesian section of \(G\).
The following proposition, whose verification is left to the reader, allows one to transcribe definition (2.4.10) into the language of (\([4]\). 6):

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.4.13)

For \(\theta : X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) to be an augmentation of effective descent relatively to \(G\), it is necessary and sufficient that the functor \(D^{o} \longrightarrow B/S\) over \(B\), defined by \(\theta\), induce an equivalence between the category of cartesian sections of \(G^{o}\) over \(B/S\) and the category of cartesian sections of \(G^{o}\) over \(D^{o}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary (2.4.14)

Suppose that the finite fibre products are representable in \(B\) and let \(f : R \to S\) be a morphism: for the augmented semi-simplicial object \([R\,|_f\,S]\) (cf. (1.2.7)) to be of effective descent relatively to \(G\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(f\) be a morphism of effective descent for the fibred category \(G^{o}\) over \(B\).
This follows from (2.4.13) and from (\([4] - 9\)).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.4.15)

Suppose that the finite fibre products are representable in \(B\) and let \(f : R \to S\) be a morphism. We shall say that \(f\) is a morphism of cohomological \(i\)-descent relatively to \(G\) (\(i = 1, 2\)) if the augmented semi-simplicial object \([R\,|_f\,S]\) is of cohomological \(i\)-descent relatively to \(G\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition (2.4.16)

Suppose that the finite fibre products are representable in \(B\) and let \(\theta : X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) be an augmentation: we shall say that \(\theta\) is an augmentation of universal cohomological \(i\)-descent (\(i = 1, 2\)) relatively to \(G\) if, for every morphism \(T \longrightarrow S\), the augmentation \(X_T \xrightarrow{\ \theta_T\ } C_T^D\) obtained by base change is an augmentation of cohomological \(i\)-descent relatively to \(G\).
The notion of morphism of universal cohomological \(i\)-descent relatively to \(G\) is deduced immediately from the two preceding definitions.
We shall often use the terminology "augmentation of cohomological \(G\)-\(i\)-descent" in place of "augmentation of cohomological \(i\)-descent relatively to \(G\)".
2.5 The descent spectral sequence

(2.5.1) Let \(A\) be an abelian category. We denote by \(F(A)\) the category whose objects are the objects of \(A\), equipped with a discrete and codiscrete filtration, and whose morphisms are the filtered morphisms of \(A\): the category \(F(A)\) is an additive category (but not abelian).

The category \(K(F(A))\) of filtered complexes of \(A\), with discrete and codiscrete filtration degree by degree, is a triangulated category and the canonical functors \[ (2.5.1.1) \qquad \mathrm{Gr}_n : K(F(A)) \longrightarrow K(A) \] are triangulated. The set \(\Sigma\) of morphisms \(f\) of \(K(F(A))\) such that \(\mathrm{Gr}_n(f)\) is a quasi-isomorphism for every \(n\) is therefore a saturated multiplicative system [cf. [9]. §2. n°1].

By inverting the arrows of this system, we obtain a new triangulated category denoted \(\mathrm{D}\,F(A)\) and the functors \(\mathrm{Gr}_n\) extend to functors \[ (2.5.1.2) \qquad \mathrm{Gr}_n : \mathrm{D}\,F(A) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}(A) . \]
In what follows we shall consider only complexes bounded below: we naturally introduce the notations \(K^+(F(A))\) and \(\mathrm{D}^+F(A)\).

(2.5.2) Let \(B\) be a thick subcategory of \(A\) and let us denote by \(K_B^+(F(A))\) the full subcategory of \(K^+(F(A))\) whose objects are the complexes \(X'\) such that \(H^i(\mathrm{Gr}_j(X')) \in B\) for every pair of integers \((i, j)\): \(K_B^+(F(A))\) is a localizing triangulated subcategory of \(K(F(A))\) [cf. [7]. (I. §5)]. We shall denote by \(\mathrm{D}_B^+F(A)\) the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{D}\,F(A)\) whose objects are the complexes bounded below \(X'\) such that \(H^i(\mathrm{Gr}_j(X')) \in B\) for every pair \((i, j)\): by (loc. cit.), \(\mathrm{D}_B^+F(A)\) is identified with the category of fractions \(K_B^+(F(A))_\Sigma \cap K_B^+(F(A))\).

The "forgetting of filtrations" functor: \[ \iota : K^+(F(A)) \longrightarrow K^+(A) \] is triangulated. Moreover, it follows from \([[5]. I. (4.7)]\) that \(\iota(f)\) is a quasi-isomorphism if \(f \in \Sigma\) and that \(\iota(K_B^+(F(A)) \subset K_B^+(A))\). The functor \(\iota\) thus extends to a triangulated functor \[ (2.5.2.1) \qquad \iota : \mathrm{D}^+F(A) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}^+(A) \] such that \(\iota(\mathrm{D}_B^+F(A)) \subset \mathrm{D}_B^+(A)\).

Let us note finally that there exists a canonical spectral functor \(\mathrm{D}_B^+F(A) \to B\), abutting to \(H^n \circ \iota\), and whose \(E_1\) term is given by \(H^{p+q} \circ \mathrm{Gr}_p\) [cf. [5] I. (4.2)].
We now return to the notations of (2.3) assuming \(D = \Delta\): \(Z'\) will denote the complex of \(\mathrm{Add}(\Delta)\) defined by (2.3.9.1).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.5.3)

Let \((S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) be a ringed topos. The functor \(\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} : \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S) \to \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) possesses a canonical factorization \[ \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S) \xrightarrow{\ {}^{F}\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*}\ } \mathrm{D}^+F(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ } \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \] Moreover, for every integer \(i\), the following diagram is commutative: \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times D), \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{R}^+(e_i^*)} \ar[dr]_-{{}^{F}\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*}} & & \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \\ & \mathrm{D}^+F(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[ur]_-{\mathrm{Gr}_i} & } \]

Consider the functor \(C^+(C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)) \xrightarrow{\ (\ )_s\ } C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\): if \(X''\) is an object of \(C^+(C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S))\), we equip \((X'')_s\) with its second canonical filtration [cf. [5]. I.4.8]; we thus obtain a factorization: \[ (2.5.3.1) \qquad (\ )_s : C^+(C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)) \longrightarrow C^+(F(S, \mathcal{O}_S)) \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ } C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \] which passes to the categories \(K^+\): \[ (2.5.3.2) \qquad (\ )_s : K^+(C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)) \longrightarrow K^+(F(S, \mathcal{O}_S)) \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ } K^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \] since a homotopy of \(C^+(C^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S))\) induces a filtered homotopy.

We then have a diagram: \[ (2.5.3.3) \qquad \xymatrix@R=1.6em@C=2.4em{ \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times \Delta), \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*}} \ar@{-->}[dr] & & \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \\ & \mathrm{D}^+F(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[ur]_-{\iota} & \\ & K^+(F(S, \mathcal{O}_S)) \ar[u] \ar[dr]^-{\iota} & \\ K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times \Delta), \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[uuu] \ar[ur] \ar[rr]_-{(\ )_s \circ K^+(\varepsilon_{Z'*})} & & K^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[uuu] } \] and one verifies that there exists a functor \[ {}^{F}\mathrm{R}^+\varepsilon_{Z'*} : \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(S \times \Delta), \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}^+F(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \] and only one making (2.5.3.3) commutative.
The rest of the proposition is obvious.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.5.4)

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed semi-simplicial topos and \(\theta : (E, A) \longrightarrow (S \times \Delta, \mathcal{O}_S)\) an augmentation: for every integer \(i\), we denote by \(\theta_i : (E_i, A_i) \to (S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) the morphism of ringed topos induced by \(\theta\) over \(i\).

The functor \(\mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_* : \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) possesses a canonical factorization \[ \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \xrightarrow{\ {}^{F}\mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_*\ } \mathrm{D}^+F(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ } \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \] such that for every integer \(i\), the canonical diagram \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{R}^+ e_i^*} \ar[d]_{{}^{F}\mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_*} & & \mathrm{D}^+(E_i, A_i) \ar[d]^{\mathrm{R}^+\theta_{i*}} \\ \mathrm{D}^+F(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[rr]_-{\mathrm{Gr}_i} & & \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) } \] is essentially commutative.
Follows from what precedes and from (1.3.12).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.5.5)

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed semi-simplicial topos and \(\theta : (E, A) \longrightarrow (S \times \Delta, \mathcal{O}_S)\) an augmentation of cohomological 1-descent. Let \(H : (S, \mathcal{O}_S) \longrightarrow (R, \mathcal{O}_R)\) be a morphism of ringed topoi. Then there exists a spectral functor from \({}'\mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)\) to \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(R, \mathcal{O}_R)\): \[ E_1^{pq} = \mathrm{R}^q(H \circ \theta_p)_* \circ \mathrm{L}^+\theta_p^* \Longrightarrow \mathrm{R}^{p+q}H_* \] called the descent spectral functor.

Let \(H \circ \theta : (E, A) \longrightarrow (R \times \Delta, \mathcal{O}_R)\) be the augmentation canonically deduced from \(\theta\) by composition with \(H\); we have \[ (2.5.5.1) \qquad \overline{(H \circ \theta)}_* = H_* \circ \overline{\theta}_* \] so that the diagram \[ (2.5.5.2) \qquad \xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=2.4em{ \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*)} \ar[dr]_-{\mathrm{R}^+H_*} & & \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \ar[dl]^-{\mathrm{R}^+\overline{(H \circ \theta)}_*} \\ & \mathrm{D}^+(R, \mathcal{O}_R) & } \] is essentially commutative.

\((\mathrm{R}^+\overline{(H \circ \theta)}_* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{R}^+H_* \circ \mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_*\) and \(\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S)} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{R}^+\overline{\theta}_* \circ \mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*))\). Thanks to (2.5.4), for every \(i\) we have an essentially commutative diagram: \[ (2.5.5.3) \qquad \xymatrix@R=2.4em@C=2.6em{ \mathrm{D}^+(S, \mathcal{O}_S) \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{L}^+\overline{\theta}^*} \ar[ddr]_-{\mathrm{R}^+H_*} & \mathrm{D}^+(\underline{\Gamma}(E), A) \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{R}^+(e_i^*)} \ar[d]|-{{}^{F}\mathrm{R}^+\overline{(H \circ \theta)}_*} & \mathrm{D}^+(E_i, A_i) \ar[d]^-{\mathrm{R}^+(H \circ \theta_i)_*} \\ & \mathrm{D}^+F(R, \mathcal{O}_R) \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{Gr}_i} \ar[d]_-{\iota} & \mathrm{D}^+(R, \mathcal{O}_R) \\ & \mathrm{D}^+(R, \mathcal{O}_R) & } \] The announced spectral functor is obtained by considering the canonical spectral functor on \(\mathrm{D}^+F(R, \mathcal{O}_R)\), which we compose with \({}^{F}\mathrm{R}^+\overline{(H \circ \theta)}_* \circ \mathrm{L}^+(\overline{\theta}^*)\).
We leave it to the reader to verify the following proposition:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.5.6)

With the preceding notation, the term \(E_2^{pq}\) of the preceding spectral functor is written: \[ \check{H}^p \circ \mathrm{R}^q((H \circ \theta)_*) \circ \mathrm{L}^+\overline{\theta}^* \] where \(\check{H}^p : \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(R \times \Delta), \mathcal{O}_R) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(R, \mathcal{O}_R)\) is the functor which associates to every functor \(\Delta \xrightarrow{\ F\ } \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(R, \mathcal{O}_R)\) the homology object in degree \(p\) of the associated complex (denoted \(\varepsilon_{Z'*}(F)'\) in (2.3.3)).

We now return to the terminology introduced in (2.4): thanks to the sorites (2.5.2), all the preceding considerations will transcribe word for word by placing the letter \(G\) as a subscript wherever this makes sense. The details are left to the reader; we obtain in particular:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (2.5.7)

Let \(\theta : X \longrightarrow C_S^D\) be an augmentation of cohomological 1-descent relatively to \(G\) and let \(h : S \longrightarrow R\) be a morphism of \(B\); there exists a spectral functor from \(\mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)\) to \(G_R\): \[ E_1^{pq} = \mathrm{R}_G^q(h \circ \theta)_* \circ \mathrm{L}_G^+\theta_p^* \Longrightarrow \mathrm{R}_G^{p+q}h_* \] with \(E_2^{pq} = \check{H}^p \circ \mathrm{R}_G^q\underline{\Gamma}((h \circ \theta)_*) \circ \mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{\theta}^*\).

footnotes.html: (∗) for every complex \(K'\), \(K'[-n]\) denotes the complex \(T^{-n}(K')\), where \(T\) is the translation functor.
(∗) For every abelian category \(A\), the letter \(Q\) denotes the canonical functor \(K^+(A) \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}^+(A)\).

blocks.html: 3. Descent criteria
3.0 Notations
In all that follows, we shall retain the notations of (2.4). We shall always assume that the finite fibre products are representable in \(B\).
We shall assume moreover that \(B\) satisfies the following condition:
(3.0.0) Direct sums exist in \(B\), are disjoint, universal and are families of effective descent and of effective \(G^{o}\)-descent [cf. [4] (9.23) (9.25) and (9.27)].
(3.0.1) Let us now recall some classical notations concerning the objects semi-simplicial of a category [cf. ([3] Chap. II) and (V. appendix)].
Let \(E\) be a category possessing finite projective limits; \(\Delta^{o}E\) denotes the category of semi-simplicial objects of \(E\) (cf. (1.2.6)).

Let \(n\) be an integer: we denote by \(\Delta_n\) (resp. \(\Delta_n^+\), \(\Delta_n^-\)) the full subcategory of \(\Delta\) (resp. \(\Delta^+\), \(\Delta^-\)) formed by the objects \([p]\) such that \(p \leq n\).

The restriction functor \[ (3.0.1.1) \qquad i_n^* : \Delta^{o}E \longrightarrow \Delta_n^{o}E \] possesses a right adjoint \(i_{n*}\), since the finite projective limits exist in \(E\) (cf. (1.2.10)). We denote by \(\mathrm{cosk}_n\), and call the coskeleton functor of order \(n\), the functor \(i_{n*} \circ i_n^*\); by abuse of notation, we shall also use the notation \(\mathrm{cosk}_n\) for the functor \(i_{n*}\).

For every integer \(p\), let us denote by \(\Delta_{n[p]}\) (resp. \(\Delta_{n[p]}^+\)) the full subcategory \(\Delta_{[p]}\) (resp. \(\Delta_{[p]}^+\)) of the objects of \(\Delta\) (resp. \(\Delta^+\)) over \([p]\), defined by the objects \([q]\) over \([p]\) such that \(q \leq n\); we leave it to the reader to verify that we have: \[ (3.0.1.2) \qquad (\mathrm{cosk}_n(X))_p = \varprojlim_{\Delta_{n[p]}} X_q \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{\Delta_{n[p]}^+} X_q \]

(3.0.2) Let \(X\) and \(X'\) be two objects of \(\Delta^{o}E\) and \(f, g : X \rightrightarrows X'\) two morphisms. A homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\) consists in the datum, for every \(n\), of a map \(h_n : \mathrm{Hom}_\Delta([n], [1]) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_E(X_n, X'_n)\) satisfying the two following conditions:
\[ (3.0.2.1) \qquad h_n(\partial^1) = f_n \quad \text{and} \quad h_n(\partial^{o}) = g_n \quad \text{for all } n. \]

(3.0.2.2) for every arrow \([n] \longrightarrow [p]\) in \(\Delta\), we have a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix@R=2.5em@C=2.5em{ \mathrm{Hom}_\Delta([p], [1]) \ar[r] \ar[dd] & \mathrm{Hom}_E(X_p, X'_p) \ar[dr] & \\ & & \mathrm{Hom}_E(X_p, X'_p) \\ \mathrm{Hom}_\Delta([n], [1]) \ar[r] & \mathrm{Hom}_E(X_n, X'_n) \ar[ur] & } \]

N.B.: The relation thus introduced on the set of morphisms from \(X\) to \(X'\) is not an equivalence relation; one can remedy this drawback by introducing the notion of composite homotopy [cf. [3] chap. III]: we shall not use this latter notion.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (3.0.2.3)

Let \(X\) and \(X'\) be two objects of \(\Delta^{o}E\), \(f, g : X \rightrightarrows X'\) two morphisms and \(F : E \to C\) a functor where \(C\) is an abelian category. A simplicial homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\) induces a homotopy on the morphisms of cochain complexes canonically associated with \(F(f)\) and \(F(g)\).
We are reduced to the case where \(C\) is the category of modules over a ring, and we apply \([[5] I. (3.7.1)]\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma (3.0.2.4)

Let \(n\) be an integer, \(X\) and \(X'\) two objects of \(\Delta_n^{o}E\). Let \(f\) and \(g\) be two morphisms from \(X\) to \(X'\) such that \(f_p = g_p\) for \(p < n\): then there exists a simplicial homotopy from \(\mathrm{cosk}_n(f)\) to \(\mathrm{cosk}_n(g)\).

We define \(h_p : \mathrm{Hom}_\Delta([p], [1]) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(X_p, X'_p)\) by the constant map with value \(f_p = g_p\) for \(p < n\), then \(h_n : \mathrm{Hom}_\Delta([n], [1]) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(X_n, X'_n)\) by sending all the elements of \(\mathrm{Hom}_\Delta([n], [1])\), except \(\partial^{o}\), to \(f_n\), and \(\partial^{o}\) to \(g_n\). We then observe that \(\mathrm{Hom}_\Delta([k], [1]) = \varprojlim_{\substack{[q] \to [k] \\ q \geq n}} \mathrm{Hom}([q], [1])\) for \(k > n\), which allows us to define \(h_k\) canonically.
3.1 Comparison of two augmentations from the point of view of cohomological 1-descent

Let \(S\) be an object of \(B\): we denote by \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{plat}}(D^{o}, B/S)\) the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Hom}(D^{o}, B/S)\) whose objects are the flat augmentations [cf. (1.2.6) and (2.4.3.1)].

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition (3.1.1)

Let \(X \xrightarrow{\ u\ } C_S^D\) and \(X' \xrightarrow{\ u'\ } C_S^D\) be two objects of \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{plat}}(D^{o}, B/S)\). Let \(f : X \longrightarrow X'\) be a morphism over \(S\) (i.e. a morphism of \(\mathrm{Hom}(D^{o}, B/S)\)); to it there corresponds in a natural way a functorial morphism \[ \eta_G^f : \mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{u}'_* \circ \mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{u}'^* \longrightarrow \mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{u}_* \circ \mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{u}^* \] such that the following diagram commutes: \[ \xymatrix@R=2.5em@C=3em{ & \mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{u}'_* \circ \mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{u}'^* \ar[dd]^{\eta_G^f} \\ 1_{\mathrm{D}_{G_S}^+(S)} \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & \\ & \mathrm{R}_G^+\overline{u}_* \circ \mathrm{L}_G^+\overline{u}^* } \]
Moreover, if \(D = \Delta\), then \(\eta_G^f\) depends only on the homotopy class (cf. (3.0.2)) of \(f\) in \(\mathrm{Hom}(\Delta^{o}, B/S)\).
It is clear that we may assume that \(G = \underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}^{o}, \mathfrak{G})\) for the construction of \(\eta_G^f\).

Let \(I\) be the category defined by the diagram type \[ (3.1.1.1) \qquad 0 \longrightarrow 1 \] We denote by \(r_o : D \longrightarrow I \times D\) (resp. \(r_1\)) the fully faithful functor defined by \(r_o(i) = (0, i)\) (resp. \(r_1(i) = (1, i)\)).

By virtue of the canonical isomorphism \[ (3.1.1.2) \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}((I \times D)^{o}, B/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I^{o}, \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(D^{o}, B/S)) \] the data of (3.1.1) define a flat augmentation \[ (3.1.1.3) \qquad [X\,|_f\,X'] \xrightarrow{\ ufu'\ } C_S^{I \times D} \]

Let \(F\) be an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}_S^{o}, \mathfrak{G}_S)\); the canonical morphism \[ (3.1.1.4) \qquad e_{I \times D}^*(F) \longrightarrow \underline{\Gamma}((ufu')_*) \circ \underline{\Gamma}((ufu')^*)(e_{I \times D}^*(F)) \] may be interpreted as a commutative triangle in \(\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\underline{\Gamma}(\overline{C_S^D}), \mathfrak{G})\): \[ (3.1.1.5) \qquad \xymatrix@R=2.5em@C=3em{ & \underline{\Gamma}(u'_*) \circ \underline{\Gamma}(u'^*)(e_D^*(F)) \ar[dd] \\ e_D^*(F) \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & \\ & \underline{\Gamma}(u_*) \circ \underline{\Gamma}(u^*)(e_D^*(F)) } \] whence a functorial morphism \(\overline{u}'_* \circ \overline{u}'^* \xrightarrow{\ \alpha_f\ } \overline{u}_* \circ \overline{u}^*\) such that the diagram \[ (3.1.1.6) \qquad \xymatrix@R=2.5em@C=3em{ & \overline{u}'_* \circ \overline{u}'^* \ar[dd]^{\alpha_f} \\ 1_{\underline{\mathrm{Mod}}(\mathscr{E}_S^{o}, \mathfrak{G}_S)} \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & \\ & \overline{u}_* \circ \overline{u}^* } \] commutes.

We consequently obtain a functorial morphism such that the diagram \[ (3.1.1.7) \qquad \xymatrix@R=2.5em@C=3em{ & K^+(\overline{u}'_*) \circ K^+(\overline{u}'^*) \ar[dd]^{K^+(\alpha_f)} \\ 1_{K^+(\mathscr{E}_S^{o}, \mathfrak{G}_S)} \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & \\ & K^+(\overline{u}_*) \circ K^+(\overline{u}^*) } \] commutes.

(Let us remark that \(K^+(\alpha_f)\) can also be obtained formally by adjunction using the isomorphism \(K^+(\underline{\Gamma}(f^*)) \circ K^+(\overline{u}'^*) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } K^+(\overline{u}^*)\)).

Let \(F'\) be a complex of \(K^+(S)\) and \(\xi : K^+(\overline{ufu'}^*)(F') \to J'\) a quasi-isomorphism such that, for every integer \(n\), \(J^n\) is totally acyclic object by object (cf. (1.3.13)).
